Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

1

set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

A A PPENDIX

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

across repeated runs. We use the same membership inference attack as in Chundawat et al. (2023a);
Foster et al. (2023), where logistic regression is used to classify samples as seen or unseen for a
given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.

1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch

key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset
of data in percent. Since SSD (and therefore LFSSD) is deterministic, there is no standard deviation

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2

*Indicates equal contribution

excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.
excerpts.heading: 2 M ETHODS & R ESULTS

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution

excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

We build upon the approach presented in SSD (Foster et al., 2023). Given the parameter importance
over both D and Df , we can select parameters that are disproportionately important for the forget

of the gradient. For multi-dimensional outputs, this gradient must be calculated over every dimen-

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain
column (Shokri et al., 2017). Similarity to the retrained model is necessary, as ”over-forgetting” can
lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

LOSS -FREE MACHINE UNLEARNING

Jack Foster∗1,2, Stefan Schoepf ∗1,2 & Alexandra Brintrup 1,2
1Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge
2The Alan Turing Institute
*Indicates equal contribution
{jwf40,ss2823,ab702}@cam.ac.uk
excerpts.heading: Accepted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2024 (Preprint)

excerpts.text:
ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.
Most existing machine unlearning approaches require a model to be fine-tuned
to remove information while preserving performance. This is computationally
expensive and necessitates the storage of the whole dataset for the lifetime of
the model. Retraining-free approaches often utilise Fisher information, which
is derived from the loss and requires labelled data which may not be available.
Thus, we present an extension to the Selective Synaptic Dampening algorithm,
substituting the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix for the gradient of the
l2 norm of the model output to approximate sensitivity. We evaluate our method
in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show
our label-free method is competitive with existing state-of-the-art approaches.
excerpts.heading: ABSTRACT

excerpts.text:
1 I NTRODUCTION & RELATED WORK

With increasing regulations around machine learning, the ability for a trained model to forget private
or harmful information is essential. This task is typically formulated by splitting some training
dataset D into a subset of data that needs to be forgotten Df , and the retained data Dr = D \ Df .
The objective is to forget Df from the model, while simultaneously preserving model performance
on Dr (Cao & Yang, 2015). To solve this problem, several methods have been proposed that disrupt
the model’s functional mapping for samples in Df (e.g. by learning random labels), while also
training for a small number of epochs over Dr to repair or protect performance (Chundawat et al.,
2023a;b; Graves et al., 2021; Tarun et al., 2023; Kurmanji et al., 2023). This is computationally
expensive and requires the storage of the full dataset permanently. In contrast, recent methods such
as FisherForgetting from Golatkar et al. (2020) or Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) from Foster
et al. (2023) have explored retraining-free approaches, with the latter achieving state-of-the-art
performance. These often involve estimating the importance of parameters for the forget set,
allowing them to be disrupted through noise or dampening, but without destroying performance
on the retain set. Parameter importance estimation is typically achieved via the diagonal of the
Fisher information matrix (FIM), which in practice is calculated as the square of the first-order
gradients of the loss. This requires access to a ground truth label, which may not always be
available. Therefore, we propose a novel extension of SSD that does not require access to the loss
or ground truth labels, which we refer to as Loss-Free Selective Synaptic Dampening (LFSSD).
LFSSD replaces the Fisher-based importance estimation with an approximation of the sensitivity of
the model to perturbations of each parameter, which may be interpreted as parameter importance.
Such importance estimation has been shown to be effective in continual learning (Aljundi et al.,
2018), yet it has not been applied in unlearning. Here, we show this new approach to dampening
important parameters is equally effective as Fisher information, without relying on labelled data.
To the best of our knowledge, LFSSD is the first retraining-free unlearning method to require only
the unlabelled forget samples at forgetting time.

Which we can calculate over D and Df and substitute into equation 1 in place of [] and []f . Results
can be seen in Table 1, with further results available in the appendix. The objective is to maximise
the Dr accuracy while having a low membership inference attack score (MIA) similar to the retrain

lead to the Streisand effect (e.g., labelling a cat as a boat is an obvious modification) (Chundawat
et al., 2023a). The results show that LFSSD produces scores similar to that of a model trained
on only Dr, and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods such as SSD, while being the first
method to require no labelled data and no retraining. A shared limitation with SSD is the reliance
on choosing α and λ values that balance forgetting and model performance.

excerpts.text:
3 C ONCLUSION

Developing lightweight yet effective machine unlearning approaches is a significant open problem.
In this work, we presented a novel extension of existing literature that is the first retraining free
machine unlearning method to require only the unlabelled input samples for the forget set. By not
requiring the long-term storage of the retain dataset, a labelled forget set, or the loss over the forget
set, LFSSD is lightweight, robust and more practically useful than its predecessors.

Benchmarks. We evaluate LFSSD in the same manner as Chundawat et al. (2023a); Foster et al.
(2023), comparing against a baseline model without any unlearning, a model retrained from scratch
on only Dr, a model finetuned for 2 epochs on Dr, and several existing state-of-the-art methods
(Chundawat et al., 2023a; Graves et al., 2021; Foster et al., 2023) (teacher, amnesiac, SSD). Three
key tasks are evaluated using ResNet18 (RN) and Vision Transformer (ViT): full class, subclass,
and random forgetting. Fullclass entails forgetting an entire class from the dataset (e.g. rocket from
Cifar100), subclass involves forgetting a related subclass from the dataset (e.g. all rockets from class
Vehicle2 in Cifar20), and random forgetting selects a random subset of samples across all classes.
Datasets used include the Cifar suite (Krizhevsky & Hinton, 2010), and the PINS face recognition
dataset (Burak, 2020). Runs are repeated 10 times for each method, with the mean and standard
deviation shown in the tables. Dr and Df in the tables denote the accuracy on the respective subset

given model, based the entropy of the model outputs for that sample.

Resources. A single backward pass over the full dataset D is O(bf ull· p) where bf ullis the number
of batches in the dataset and p is the number of parameters in the model. Similarly, the complexity
for the forget and retain set is O(bf orget· p) and O(bretain · p), respectively. Note that bretain ≈
bf ull>> bf orget. SSD requires only one computation of the gradients for D (can be saved and
reused), then for every forget request it requires one computation forDf to then apply the dampening
in O(bf orget· p).

LFSSD has the same complexity as SSD with the difference being that LFSSD calculates the norm
of the output instead of the loss. In practice, this is similar in compute time.

Other methods are retraining-based and depend on the number of epochs N, generally on the order
of O(N · bretain · p), which is much larger.

Sensitivity analysis. The values for alpha and lambda for SSD are taken from Foster et al. (2023)
where the authors used Optuna to search for ideal parameters. For LFSSD we performed a simplified
hyperparameter search keeping lambda fixed at 1 and alpha values [1, 50]. We pick one value per
unlearning task (e.g. full class, sub-class, random) to show robustness across classes and do not
use the best alpha per individual class/subclass (e.g., taking alpha 25 for rocket, alpha 5 for another
class, etc.). A sensitivity analysis in Table 2 on CIFAR100 rocket class unlearning shows that there
is a significant drop off in performance when picking an alpha that is too aggressive or conservative
but the method has a wide plateau in which it performs well.

Unlearning scenarios without labels. For cases where labels are hard to get we expect two main
scenarios: First, having a catalogue of undesired/copyrighted data (e.g., images) that we want to
unlearn from the model just to be on the safe side legally even if it might not be in the model. In this
case, we do not have the labels. Second, models that were trained with semi-supervised learning
could benefit from our method when we do not want to rely on the accuracy of pseudo labels.

synthesis.contribution_summary: The paper proposes LFSSD, a variant of Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD) that replaces the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix with the gradient of the squared l2 norm of the model output, a sensitivity estimate taken from Aljundi et al. (2018). SSD's parameter-selection and dampening rule is otherwise kept. As a result, unlearning needs neither retraining nor labels, only the unlabelled forget samples. Experiments cover full-class, subclass, random-sample and face unlearning on ResNet and ViT models, with comparisons to SSD, retraining and other baselines.
synthesis.originality: The originality is incremental but clearly positioned. The authors credit the importance estimator to prior continual-learning work (Aljundi et al., 2018) and reuse the SSD selection rule. The new element is moving this estimator into unlearning and the label-free capability that follows. This is a modest, honestly attributed change that suits a tiny-paper scope. The claim to be the first retraining-free, label-free method is hedged in the introduction ('to the best of our knowledge') but stated without the hedge in the conclusion. The paper also cites zero-shot machine unlearning (Chundawat et al., 2023b) only within a list of retraining-based methods and never says how its label or data requirements differ. The primacy claim therefore cannot yet be checked against the paper's own citations. This review has not verified that cited work.
synthesis.likely_impact: Practitioners who must remove data whose labels are unavailable could benefit, for example in copyrighted-data catalogues or semi-supervised models. The method is simple, lightweight and easy to adopt for anyone already using SSD. Several factors may limit its influence. The method is a small change to an existing algorithm. Its results are competitive rather than uniformly equal to SSD. Most importantly, it is unclear how α would be chosen in a truly label-free deployment, since the per-task tuning described appears to depend on accuracy on Dr and a retrained reference. If those require labels, the practical label-free benefit is qualified, although the importance estimate itself remains label-free.
synthesis.decision_synthesis: In favour: the contribution is simple, clearly motivated and honestly attributed. Across the appendix tables, LFSSD is broadly comparable to SSD and the other baselines on full-class, subclass, random and face tasks, which supports the claim that it is competitive. Against: several pieces of evidence matter most. (1) The wording of the central claims, 'equally effective as Fisher information', 'robust' and 'similar to a model trained on only Dr', goes beyond mixed per-setting results. In some subclass cells LFSSD over-forgets relative to the retrained model, which the paper itself treats as a Streisand-effect risk (e.g., ViT 'sea' Df 20.83 vs 95.12 retrained; RN 'sea' 18.06 vs 91.47). In other cells it forgets less than SSD (e.g., ViT mushroom Df 31.42 vs 6.68). (2) The two methods were tuned differently. SSD reuses α values from prior tuning, while LFSSD's α was chosen per task (10, 5, 3.5) through a simplified search whose guiding data split is not stated. Performance is sharply sensitive at the ends of the α range (α=1 drops Dr accuracy to 16.87%). (3) SSD and LFSSD are reported with ±0.00 while the other baselines show non-zero spread. This suggests, though it is not confirmed, that the two were run deterministically on one fixed model. If so, the error bars are not comparable and do not show sensitivity to the original model. Score-changing questions for the authors: how would α be selected without labels or a retrained reference? Which data guided the α search? What variance across trained models do SSD and LFSSD have? How does LFSSD differ from zero-shot unlearning (Chundawat et al., 2023b) in its requirements? Non-blocking improvements: restore the hedge on the primacy claim in the conclusion, soften the 'equally effective' and 'robust' wording, and limit the 'similar to retrain' framing to the settings where it holds.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: The authors define success as similarity to the retrained model. In the ViT subclass rows (sea Df; baby MIA), retrain scores 95.12 and 77.37, while LFSSD scores 20.83 and 1.60. By the authors' own standard, this is over-forgetting. SSD tracks retrain more closely in these same rows. For ViT on Cifar100 lamp, the Df row shows retrain at 0.00, LFSSD at 0.00 and SSD at 36.89. The Dr row shows LFSSD retaining accuracy at SSD's level for both architectures. Class-unlearning rows show LFSSD with Df at 0, matching retrain. In the ViT mushroom subclass row, LFSSD's Df is 31.42, versus 6.68 for SSD and 26.57 for retrain. Results therefore vary by setting.
points: The claim that LFSSD scores are similar to retraining is overstated for subclass unlearning. In several cells LFSSD departs substantially from the retrained model, which is the authors' own target.
On full-class unlearning, the results support the claim that LFSSD is comparable to SSD. In one case (ViT lamp) LFSSD forgets where SSD leaves residual accuracy.
The tables support the claim that LFSSD is competitive with SSD on class unlearning. The introduction's 'equally effective' framing is stronger than some subclass rows show.

significance.reasoning: The paper names storage and label requirements as practical barriers. LFSSD addresses the label barrier while inheriting SSD's one-time computation over D.
points: Removing the label requirement while keeping SSD's one-time computation over D gives a cheap, simple baseline. Researchers working on post-hoc unlearning are likely to adopt it.

originality.reasoning: The authors attribute both components to prior work. The originality therefore lies in transferring the estimator into unlearning, which removes the label requirement. The claim that it 'has not been applied in unlearning' is author-reported and was not verified here. The authors attribute both the estimator and the dampening rule to prior work. What they claim as new is the combination and its use in unlearning. Whether the estimator has truly not been used in unlearning before is author-reported and was not independently verified.
points: The method makes one targeted substitution: it replaces SSD's Fisher-based importance with the output-norm sensitivity estimate from Aljundi et al. (2018). The authors frame this as an extension and credit the source of the importance measure.

The authors present the novelty as transferring an existing importance estimator into unlearning, not as a new estimator. This transfer framing is consistent with the methods section. The originality is therefore incremental: a recombination of SSD with the estimator of Aljundi et al.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: The semi-supervised and copyright-catalogue scenarios are motivations, not experiments. All reported benchmarks use labelled datasets: Cifar and PINS. Equation 3 uses only the output norm, so neither labels nor retraining are needed. Robustness to alpha, however, is shown on a single class (Table 2), and the alpha value differs per task. The authors also acknowledge their reliance on alpha and lambda.
points: The practicality claims ('robust, more practically useful') rest on argument. The label-free scenarios the paper describes are not evaluated.
The retraining-free, label-free property follows directly from the method's construction and is supported. The 'robust' part of the conclusion relies on limited hyperparameter evidence.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The paper cites a zero-shot unlearning work but groups it with retraining-based methods. It never states that work's label requirements. I did not inspect the cited work.
points: The primacy claim is hedged in the introduction but stated without the hedge in the conclusion. The paper does not distinguish its label requirements from those of cited zero-shot unlearning work.

ABSTRACT

We present a machine unlearning approach that is both retraining- and label-free.

claim_support.reasoning: No claims are linked to this contribution, so its claim support cannot be traced.

significance.reasoning: No grounded, candidate-targeted finding for this axis.

originality.reasoning: The authors say the importance estimator comes from Aljundi et al. They also say the SSD selection rule (Eq. 1) is reused. The original element is therefore the transfer of this estimator into unlearning, which removes the need for labels. This is a modest but clearly stated delta, appropriate to a tiny-paper scope. The first quote concedes that the estimator comes from prior work, so the originality lies in combining it with SSD and in the resulting label-free capability. That framing is consistent across the paper. Whether no prior retraining-free label-free method exists (e.g., relative to the authors' account of zero-shot unlearning, Chundawat et al. 2023b) is author-reported and was not verified here. The authors state the novelty precisely as an extension and openly credit the importance measure to prior work, so the framing does not overreach. The 'first' claim is hedged. It was not verified against the literature. The introduction says 'to the best of our knowledge', but the conclusion drops that hedge. Chundawat et al. 2023b (zero-shot unlearning) is grouped with retraining-based methods, but its label and data requirements are not discussed.
points: LFSSD is positioned as an extension of SSD that swaps the Fisher-diagonal importance for the output-norm sensitivity of Aljundi et al. (2018). Both components are prior work, so the novelty lies in combining them and in the label-free setting it enables.

The authors present LFSSD as an extension of their own SSD that borrows MAS-style sensitivity from continual learning. The novelty claimed is the transfer to unlearning and the label-free setting, not a new importance estimator.

The authors present originality as a novel extension of their own SSD, transferring the Aljundi et al. sensitivity measure to unlearning. They claim a 'first' that is qualified as 'to the best of our knowledge'.

The 'first label-free, retraining-free' claim is hedged in the introduction but stated unhedged in the conclusion. The paper also cites zero-shot unlearning without explaining how it differs in data or label requirements.

originality.reasoning: The paper explicitly borrows both the base algorithm and the importance measure. The originality claim is therefore limited to transferring the measure into SSD for unlearning. I have not inspected the cited works, so whether this transfer is truly new is unverified. The authors credit the estimator to prior work, so this candidate's novelty is limited to applying it in SSD. The authors directly attribute Eq. 3 to Aljundi et al. The authors attribute the estimator to Aljundi et al. (2018), whose content is reported by the authors rather than verified here.
points: The authors present the advance as combining two existing pieces: SSD (their own prior method) and the Memory Aware Synapses sensitivity measure (Aljundi et al.). The novelty is the application of that measure to unlearning, not a new importance measure.
The output-norm sensitivity measure is explicitly taken from Aljundi et al. (2018); the new element is its use as a replacement for the FIM in SSD.
The output-norm sensitivity substitution is explicitly borrowed from continual learning. Its originality is limited to applying it in the unlearning setting.
The importance estimator itself is credited to Aljundi et al. (2018), so it is not novel. The novelty is its application within SSD for unlearning.

assessments.attribution: advisory specialist findings from this review run

claim_support.reasoning: No claims are linked to this contribution, so its claim support cannot be traced. The authors set similarity to the retrained model as the success criterion. In ViT subclass 'sea', LFSSD's Df accuracy is 20.83 versus 95.12 for the retrained model, which is over-forgetting by that criterion. In ViT subclass 'baby', MIA is 1.6 for LFSSD versus 77.37 for retraining. In the ViT MR subclass row, LFSSD's Df is 31.42 versus SSD's 6.68. In the ViT Rkt class row, LFSSD's MIA is 10.60 versus SSD's 1.80. LFSSD wins in some other cells (e.g. ViT sea subclass), so the results are mixed rather than equivalent. No aggregate or statistical comparison is given, and per-task alpha was tuned. Retain accuracy and forget accuracy match or exceed SSD across several classes, two architectures and multiple tasks. Where the retrain reference retains the subclass, driving Df to 18% is over-forgetting, which the paper itself says risks the Streisand effect. Separately, tuning α only for LFSSD may favor it in the SSD comparison. Across most rows, LFSSD's Dr and Df scores are close to SSD's. In some subclass cases, though, LFSSD leaves Df higher than SSD (ViT mushroom: 31.42 vs 6.68). This means LFSSD is competitive overall but not uniformly equal to SSD.
points: The appendix tables broadly support the claim that LFSSD is competitive with SSD and the other baselines. However, LFSSD's forget-set (Df) accuracy sometimes diverges substantially from the retrained model in both directions.

Within the reported benchmarks, LFSSD is broadly comparable to SSD and the other baselines, supporting 'competitive'. However, 'equally effective as Fisher information' and 'robust' overstate mixed results.
Tables support the claim that LFSSD is competitive with SSD in class unlearning. For example, on ViT lamp LFSSD reaches Df 0.00 where SSD leaves 36.89.

Some results depart from the retrain reference, so the claim that LFSSD's scores are 'similar to that of a model trained on only Dr' needs qualifying. In subclass unlearning LFSSD sometimes over-forgets (RN sea Df 18.06 vs retrain 91.47). LFSSD's α is also tuned per task while SSD's values are reused from prior work.

The 'competitive with SOTA' claim is broadly supported across full-class, subclass, random and face tasks. However, ViT subclass forgetting is mixed, and the 'equally effective as Fisher' wording overstates this.
